why_this_tool: Apache Cassandra runs on a laptop in a container and rejects queries that the primary key does not serve, so it makes you design tables from the access patterns and feel the write-side cost of every denormalised copy.
alternatives: PostgreSQL or MySQL model entities first and normalise with joins; Amazon DynamoDB is a managed key-value store with a hash key and a sort key per item; MongoDB nests related data inside documents; Snowflake and BigQuery hold facts and dimensions for analytics, often built with dbt; Debezium streams changes out of a source store to keep copies in step.

setup.do: Start a single-node Apache Cassandra in a local container (Docker or Podman is the prerequisite) and open a cqlsh session against it.
setup.done_when: The cqlsh prompt appears and a query on the system keyspaces returns rows.

source.title: The Cassandra Query Language (CQL) | Apache Cassandra Documentation

verified.section_found: The Cassandra Query Language (CQL) | Apache Cassandra Documentation

setup.why: Every later step is typed as CQL into this shell, so you need one running node and a working prompt first. One node is enough until the last step.

setup.do: Read the CQL conventions and statement basics so you can follow the grammar notation used in the reference pages.
setup.done_when: You can explain what the optional and repeated parts of a statement grammar mean.
setup.why: The reference pages describe each statement with a compact grammar. Knowing how to read it saves time on every later step.

setup.do: Create a practice keyspace with SimpleStrategy and a replication factor of one, then switch to it with USE.
setup.done_when: DESCRIBE KEYSPACES lists the practice keyspace and the prompt shows it as the current keyspace.
setup.why: A keyspace is the container for all tables and sets replication. SimpleStrategy is the simplest choice for a single laptop node.

steps.do: Write the list of queries a hotel booking application must answer, in plain words, before drawing any table.
steps.done_when: You have a written list of at least five queries, each naming what it filters by and how the results are ordered.
steps.why: Query-first modelling starts from access patterns, not entities. This list drives every table you create in the following steps.

steps.do: Compare an entity-first, normalised sketch of the same hotel domain with the query-first one, and note where joins are replaced by duplicated columns.
steps.done_when: You have a two-column note that lists, for each query, the joins in the relational sketch and the single table that answers it in the query-first sketch.
steps.why: Seeing both shapes side by side shows what a relational design assumes that Cassandra does not offer: joins and referential integrity.

steps.do: Create one table per query with a partition key that groups the rows read together and clustering columns that set their order inside the partition.
steps.done_when: DESCRIBE TABLE shows each table with its partition key and clustering order, and rows selected from one partition come back sorted by the clustering column.
steps.why: The partition key decides which node holds the data and the clustering columns decide the sort order on disk. Together they are the core of wide-column modelling.

steps.do: Create a single-table key-value design as you would for DynamoDB (a paid cloud service, so use Cassandra as the local substitute): one partition key as the hash key, one clustering column as the sort key, and static columns for attributes shared by the whole item collection.
steps.done_when: One partition holds several item types distinguished by the sort key, and a static column shows the same value on every row of that partition.
steps.why: DynamoDB key design follows the same hash key plus sort key idea, so practising it here teaches item collections and overloaded keys without a cloud account.

steps.do: Query each table through its partition key, then run a query that filters on a non-key column and read the error before trying it with ALLOW FILTERING.
steps.done_when: The key-based query returns rows, the non-key query is rejected with a filtering warning, and you can say why forcing it would scan the whole table.
steps.why: The WHERE clause rules are how Cassandra enforces query-first design. The rejected query shows exactly which access pattern your model does not serve.

steps.do: Create a storage-attached index on the non-key column and run the previously rejected query again, then compare it with building a second denormalised table for the same query.
steps.done_when: The query on the non-key column returns rows without ALLOW FILTERING, and you have noted when you would choose the index and when the extra table.

source.title: Working with Storage-attached indexing (SAI) | Apache Cassandra Documentation

steps.why: An index is the alternative to another copy of the data. Comparing the two makes the trade-off between write cost and read flexibility concrete.

steps.do: Read how an indexed write goes through the memtable, the flush and compaction, so you know what each extra index costs on the write path.
steps.done_when: You can describe in three sentences what happens to index data at write, at flush and at compaction.

source.title: Storage-attached indexing (SAI) concepts | Apache Cassandra Documentation

steps.why: Every read-side shape is paid for at write time. This section shows where that cost lands on disk and when compaction rebuilds index data.

steps.do: Write the same booking into two denormalised tables with a logged BATCH, then repeat it as two separate inserts and note what a failure between them would leave behind.
steps.done_when: Both tables return the same booking after the batch, and you can explain which copy would be stale if the second separate insert never ran.
steps.why: Denormalised copies drift apart unless the writes are grouped. A batch is the basic tool for keeping copies consistent, and it has a cost you should know.

steps.do: Create a materialized view that re-keys one base table for a second query (enable materialized views in the node configuration first if the statement is refused), update the base row and query the view.
steps.done_when: A change to a base row appears in the view under its new primary key, and you can name two limitations of views from the same page.
steps.why: A materialized view lets the server maintain a denormalised copy for you. Its limitations explain why many teams still prefer application-managed copies.

steps.do: Create a fact-style table of nightly bookings partitioned by hotel and a day bucket, with dimension attributes copied onto each row, using the datetime functions to derive the bucket.
steps.done_when: Rows for different days land in different partitions and a query for one hotel and one day returns only that day's bookings.
steps.why: Dimensional modelling separates facts from dimensions. In Cassandra the time bucket becomes part of the partition key, so the window of data read is bounded.

steps.do: Run count, sum and average over one day bucket of the fact table and compare the result with what a warehouse star schema would compute across all days.
steps.done_when: The aggregate over one partition returns the expected totals, and you have noted which analytical questions would need a warehouse instead.
steps.why: Aggregates in Cassandra work well inside one partition and poorly across many. That limit is the reason analytics usually moves to a warehouse.

steps.do: Reproduce the whole model by saving every statement in one CQL file, dropping the keyspace and replaying the file with the source command in cqlsh.
steps.done_when: After a drop and a replay, DESCRIBE KEYSPACE shows the same tables, index and view as before.
steps.why: A schema that exists only in shell history cannot be reviewed or run in CI. A single replayable file is the pinned, repeatable form of your model.

steps.do: Configure a production-like setup: start a three-node local cluster in containers and recreate the keyspace with NetworkTopologyStrategy and a replication factor of three for the datacenter.
steps.done_when: The node status shows three nodes up, the keyspace description shows NetworkTopologyStrategy with three replicas, and a read still succeeds with one node stopped.
steps.why: Production keyspaces name their datacenters and replicate each partition to several nodes. This is where partition key choices start to affect load and availability.
